hints: Focus on the type of reaction here, electrophilic addition of HBr to an unsymmetrical alkene.
Draw out $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_2CH_3$ and notice C2 is more substituted than C3, so the more stable tertiary carbocation forms at C2.
Remember Markovnikov's rule that Br ends up on the more substituted carbon, so put H on C3 and Br on C2 to name the product.
walkthrough:
**Draw the starting alkene**

Great start, let's see what we have. 2-methylpent-2-ene is $(CH_3)_2C=CH-CH_2-CH_3$.

The double bond is between C2 and C3:
$$ (CH_3)_2C=CHCH_2CH_3 $$

**Apply Markovnikov addition**

HBr adds across the double bond by electrophilic addition. $H^+$ adds first to make the most stable carbocation.

Adding $H^+$ to C3 gives a tertiary carbocation at C2, which is much more stable than adding to C2:
$$ (CH_3)_2C^+-CH_2CH_2CH_3 \text{ (tertiary, major)} $$

**Place Br and name the product**

$Br^-$ then attacks the carbocation at C2. So H goes to C3 and Br goes to C2.

This gives $CH_3-CBr(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3$, which is 2-bromo-2-methylpentane.

options.A: Not correct. 1-bromo-2-methylpentane would require Br on a terminal C1 carbon, but C1 is not even part of the double bond, so no mechanism puts Br there.
options.B: Correct. H adds to the less substituted C3 and Br adds to the more substituted C2 via the stable tertiary carbocation. This is Markovnikov addition giving 2-bromo-2-methylpentane.
options.C: Not correct. 3-bromo-2-methylpentane is the anti-Markovnikov product with Br on the less substituted secondary carbon C3. This comes from the less stable secondary carbocation, so it is minor.
options.D: Not correct. 4-bromo-2-methylpentane would place Br on C4, which is a saturated $CH_2$ group far from the double bond and cannot be involved in addition.
